Title: Diagnosis
Details: What the failing test does
- testCodec105 wraps a special input stream (Codec105ErrorInputStream) in a Base64InputStream configured for encoding (the boolean argument is true) with no line breaks (lineLength 0, separator null) and then calls read() five times. The special stream is crafted to reproduce the CODEC-105 edge case by returning 0-length reads before EOF.

Key code paths
- Base64InputStream.read() delegates to read(byte[], int, int) with a single-byte buffer and loops while the result is 0.
- Base64InputStream.read(byte[], int, int) does:
  - If Base64 has no pending data: allocate a temp buffer and call int c = in.read(buf).
  - If c > 0 and the destination array is the entire array (b.length == len), call base64.setInitialBuffer(b, offset, len).
  - Then, for encoding, call base64.encode(buf, 0, c).
  - Finally, drain encoded output with base64.readResults(b, offset, len).

Why the bug happens
- With read() (single-byte destination), the condition (c > 0 && b.length == len) is true whenever the underlying stream returns some data, so Base64.setInitialBuffer is used to point Base64’s internal output buffer at the caller’s single-byte array.
- Codec105ErrorInputStream (by design) sometimes returns 0 from read(byte[]). In this case:
  - The code still calls base64.encode(buf, 0, 0). In Base64.encode, inAvail == 0 produces no output and leaves Base64’s state unchanged. Crucially, the “initial buffer” set previously remains pointing at the single-byte destination.
  - readResults then returns 0 (no data), so Base64InputStream loops and tries again.
- When the underlying stream eventually signals EOF (c == -1), Base64InputStream calls base64.encode(buf, 0, -1) to flush the remainder. Base64.encode’s EOF branch emits the final 2–4 output bytes (including padding when needed).
- Because Base64’s internal output buffer is still set to the caller’s one-byte array (from an earlier c > 0 iteration), encode attempts to write multiple bytes into a 1-byte array. This triggers an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException inside Base64.encode (reported as index “2” in the bug report), after many successful reads when the flush finally occurs.

Why it only shows up after many reads
- Base64InputStream only refills/flushes when its internal buffer is empty; most read() calls are satisfied from previously encoded data. The exception surfaces only when a zero-length read leaves the initial buffer pointing at the tiny caller buffer and a later EOF triggers the final flush into that buffer. Hence, “after 10920 successful read()s” in the report.

Root cause summary
- Base64InputStream.read(byte[], int, int) mishandles zero-length reads from the underlying stream and the use of setInitialBuffer during encoding:
  - It should not call encode when c == 0 (or should treat it as “no progress” and simply continue).
  - It should not set the Base64 initial output buffer to the caller’s destination array in the encoding path unless the destination capacity is sufficient to hold all produced output; with read(), that array is only length 1, which is never safe for encoding output.

Corrective direction
- In Base64InputStream.read(byte[], int, int):
  - If c == 0, do not call Base64.encode/decode; just continue the loop to read again (similar to the existing handling for readResults() returning 0).
  - Avoid calling base64.setInitialBuffer in the encoding mode, or gate it behind a capacity check that ensures the destination array is large enough for the encoded output (which it is not for the single-byte read() case).
